abstract: Osteosarcoma, a primary malignant bone tumor predominantly affecting children and adolescents, exhibits a dismal prognosis for patients with metastatic or recurrent disease, characterized by low five-year survival rates. This poor outcome is largely attributed to the incomplete understanding of the molecular mechanisms governing osteosarcoma aggressiveness and metastasis, coupled with a paucity of effective early diagnostic biomarkers and targeted therapeutic strategies. Consequently, elucidating the critical molecular events driving osteosarcoma pathogenesis and identifying novel biomarkers are of paramount importance for improving patient outcomes. Prior research has demonstrated aberrant expression of Zinc Finger DHHC-Type Palmitoyltransferase 9 ( ZDHHC9 ) in various malignancies, but its specific function and clinical significance in osteosarcoma remain poorly defined. This study employed a comprehensive approach integrating bioinformatic analyses and experimental validation to investigate the functional role and clinical relevance of ZDHHC9 in osteosarcoma. Bioinformatic analyses (TIMER, GEPIA, TCGA databases) were utilized to examine ZDHHC9 expression across a pan-cancer landscape and its association with survival in osteosarcoma patients. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) and Western blotting were employed to analyze ZDHHC9 expression in clinical osteosarcoma specimens and cell lines. In vitro assays (CCK-8, colony formation, wound healing, Transwell, flow cytometry, and Western blotting) were performed to evaluate the impact of ZDHHC9 on osteosarcoma cell proliferation, migration, and invasion. Proteomic sequencing, molecular docking, and co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) experiments were conducted to explore the interaction between ZDHHC9 and KRAS. Western blotting was used to analyze the regulation of Raf1, ERK1/2, and p-ERK1/2 expression by ZDHHC9 and KRAS. Finally, a xenograft model was employed to assess the effect of ZDHHC9 on in vivo tumor growth. Bioinformatic analyses revealed that elevated ZDHHC9 expression correlates with poor prognosis in osteosarcoma. IHC and Western blotting confirmed significantly increased ZDHHC9 expression in osteosarcoma tissues compared to adjacent non-tumorous tissues. Upregulation of ZDHHC9 was significantly associated with elevated Ki67 levels and advanced Enneking stage, suggesting a link to tumor aggressiveness. In vitro studies demonstrated that downregulation of ZDHHC9 suppressed osteosarcoma cell proliferation, migration, and invasion, while promoting apoptosis. Conversely, upregulation of ZDHHC9 elicited opposite effects. Proteomic sequencing revealed that ZDHHC9 knockdown significantly downregulated the expression of proteins associated with the RAS/MAPK signaling pathway. Functional experiments showed that overexpression of KRAS partially abrogated the inhibitory effects of ZDHHC9 knockdown on cell proliferation, migration, and invasion. Molecular docking and Co-IP experiments confirmed a specific interaction between ZDHHC9 and KRAS, leading to activation of the RAS/MAPK signaling pathway. ZDHHC9 promotes osteosarcoma cell proliferation, migration, and invasion by enhancing KRAS-mediated activity of the RAS/MAPK signaling pathway, which promotes cell cycle progression while inhibiting apoptosis. Data are available via ProteomeXchange with identifier PXD066322. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1038/s41598-025-13787-6.

Analysis of

The TIMER database (
https://cistrome.shinyapps.io/timer/
) was utilized to analyze
ZDHHC9
expression across various malignancies. The GEPIA database (
http://gepia.cancer-pku.cn/detail.php

ZDHHC9
expression in osteosarcoma samples and patient prognosis. The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database was used to generate receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves to evaluate the potential of
ZDHHC9
expression as a prognostic biomarker for osteosarcoma. The STRING database (
https://string-db.org/
) was queried to analyze the interaction network of ZDHHC9 with proteins involved in the MAPK signaling pathway.
Proteomic sequencing and data analysis
sh-NC and sh-
ZDHHC9
-transfected 143B cells were subjected to proteomic sequencing to identify differentially expressed proteins. Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses were performed to identify signaling pathways significantly associated with
ZDHHC9
knockdown. Differentially expressed genes were selected based on |LogFC| ≥ 1 and
P
-value ≤ 0.05. A volcano plot of differentially expressed genes was generated using the online tool at
www.bioinformatics.com.cn
. A protein-protein interaction (PPI) network of differentially expressed genes was constructed using the STRING database.
Functional enrichment analysis of overlapping genes and selection of hub genes
Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) was performed using R software. Metascape (
https://metascape.org/
) was employed for gene annotation and enrichment analysis of GO terms (biological process, molecular function, cellular component) and KEGG pathways. The top ten GO terms and top twenty KEGG pathways were presented. Based on KEGG pathway enrichment results, the Ras/MAPK signaling pathway was selected for further investigation, and differentially expressed genes within this pathway were designated as hub genes. The upstream and downstream relationships and expression patterns of these hub genes within the MAPK pathway were visualized using diagrams and bar graphs.
Molecular docking and co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP)
To investigate the interaction between ZDHHC9 and KRAS, molecular docking analysis was performed using HDOCK (hdock.phys.hust.edu.cn). PDB files of ZDHHC9 and KRAS protein models predicted by AlphaFold-3 were submitted to the HDOCK server. Co-immunoprecipitation was performed using a Protein A/G Immunoprecipitation Kit (Epizyme, YJ201). Antigen-antibody-bead complexes were washed with rinsing buffer, and protein expression was detected by Western blotting. Antibody concentrations were as follows: ZDHHC9 (1:3000, 82739-1-RR), KRAS (1:1000, 12063-1-AP).
Clinical sample collection
Tumor and adjacent non-tumorous tissue specimens were collected from 40 osteosarcoma patients treated at our institution between 2018 and 2024. Informed consent was obtained from all patients, and the study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of the General Hospital of Ningxia Medical University (Ethics Number: KYLL-2024-0405). Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) staining and immunohistochemistry (IHC)
Collected tissue samples were fixed in 10% neutral buffered formalin, routinely embedded in paraffin, and sectioned for
ZDHHC9
expression analysis. Sections were stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) for pathological diagnosis and then subjected to immunohistochemical staining. Standard IHC procedures were followed to detect ZDHHC9 expression. Briefly, sections were deparaffinized in xylene, rehydrated through a graded ethanol series, and subjected to antigen retrieval in pH 6.0 citrate buffer at 95 °C for 15 min. Endogenous peroxidase activity was blocked with 3% hydrogen peroxide for 10 min at room temperature. After blocking with 5% bovine serum albumin (BSA), sections were incubated with primary antibody (1:100, Cat NO: 24046-1-AP-50, Proteintech, Wuhan, China) overnight at 4 °C. After washing with PBS, sections were incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibody (1:200, Cat NO: GB23303, Servicebio, Wuhan, China) for 1 h at room temperature. DAB was used as the chromogen, and nuclei were counterstained with hematoxylin. Stained sections were observed and imaged using a Motic microscope (Beijing, China), and staining indices were measured and calculated using Image-Pro Plus 6 software. Negative controls were performed using phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) instead of the primary antibody. ZDHHC9 staining intensity was graded as 0 (negative), 1 (weak), 2 (moderate), or 3 (strong). The percentage of positively stained cells was scored as 0 (≤ 5%), 1 (6–25%), 2 (26–50%), 3 (51–75%), and 4 (> 75%). The final staining score (0–12) was calculated by multiplying the staining intensity and percentage scores. The scores were categorized as follows: –, 0 points; +, 1–4 points; ++, 5–8 points; +++, 9–12 points.
Western blot analysis
For immunoblotting, protein lysates were prepared from tissues and cells using RIPA lysis buffer supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors. The total protein concentration of each lysate was determined via a BCA Protein Assay Kit. An equal amount of protein (30 µg) from each sample was resolved on 10% or 12% SDS-PAGE gels and subsequently transferred onto polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membranes. Following the transfer, membranes were blocked for 1 h at room temperature in 5% non-fat milk dissolved in TBST. The membranes were then probed overnight at 4 °C with specific primary antibodies. After washing three times with TBST, membranes were incubated with the corresponding secondary antibodies, and immunoreactive bands were visualized using an enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL) kit. Densitometric analysis of the bands was performed using ImageJ software. To ensure equal loading, protein levels were normalized to GAPDH. All immunoblotting experiments were conducted in triplicate, and representative blots are presented in the figures.Antibodies against ZDHHC9 (1:3000, 82739-1-RR), KRAS (1:1000, 12063-1-AP), ERK1/2 (1:2500, 83533-1-RR), and p-ERK1/2 (1:500, 80031-1-RR) were purchased from Proteintech (Wuhan, China). GAPDH (1:5000, GB15004-100) antibody was purchased from Servicebio, Wuhan, China. Antibodies against CDK4 (1:1000, DF6102), CDK6 (1:1000, DF6448), p27 (1:1000, DF6090), P21 (1:1000, DF6423), P53 (1:1000, AF0879), Snail (1:500, AF6032), Twist1 (1:500, AF4009), Cleaved-Caspase 3 (1:500, AF7022), and Cleaved-Caspase 9 (1:500, AF5240) were purchased from Affinity Biosciences (USA). Antibodies against PCNA (1:1000, A12427) and Ki-67 (1:500, A11390) were purchased from ABclonal (China). Antibody against Slug (1:500, BS79813) was purchased from Nanjing Baiaolaibo Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (China).
Real-time quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR)
The mRNA expression levels of target genes were measured by real-time quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR). Following the manufacturer’s protocol, total RNA was first isolated from cells using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen). Subsequently, cDNA was synthesized from 1 µg of total RNA with the PrimeScript
®
RT Reagent Kit (Takara Biotech). The qPCR reactions were then performed using a SYBR Green master mix (Vazyme) on a real-time PCR system. Relative gene expression was calculated using the 2
−ΔΔCt
method, with
GAPDH
serving as the endogenous control for normalization. The primer sequences used for amplification were as follows:
ZDHHC9
forward 5′-ATGGCTACACTGTTGAGGAC-3′, reverse 5′-ATTCTTGATACGAGGCGGTG-3′;
GAPDH
forward 5′-ACATCGCTCAGACACCATG-3′, reverse 5′-TGTAGTTGAGGTCAATGAAGGG-3′.
Cell culture
The human osteosarcoma cell lines 143B, U2OS, Saos-2, and MG63, the human fetal osteoblast cell line hFOB 1.19, and human spinal mesenchymal stem cells (hMSC) were all purchased from the Cell Bank of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. The osteosarcoma lines 143B, U2OS, and MG63 were maintained in high-glucose DMEM (Gibco, USA), while Saos-2 cells were grown in RPMI 1640 medium (Gibco). The hFOB 1.19 cell line was cultured in DMEM/F12 medium (Gibco) containing 2.5 mM L-glutamine and 0.3 mg/mL G418 (Sigma-Aldrich). hMSCs were cultured using a specialized hMSC Serum-Free Medium Kit. With the exception of the hMSC medium, all other culture media were supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS, Biowest), 100 U/mL penicillin, and 0.1 mg/mL streptomycin (Leagene Biotechnology). All cell lines were maintained at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO₂.
Transfection
Lentiviral vectors for knockdown and overexpression were obtained from Qingke Biotechnology Co., Ltd. These included a short hairpin RNA targeting
ZDHHC9
(sh-
ZDHHC9
), a non-targeting negative control (sh-NC), an overexpression plasmid for
ZDHHC9
(LV-
ZDHHC9
), an overexpression plasmid for
KRAS
(LV-
KRAS
), and a corresponding empty vector (LV-Control). For lentiviral transduction, osteosarcoma cells were plated in six-well plates at a density of 1 × 10^5 cells/well 24 h prior to infection. Cells were then transduced with the respective lentiviruses at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) determined by the supplier’s instructions. A rescue group was established by co-infecting cells with sh-
ZDHHC9
and LV-
KRAS
lentiviruses. Following a 12-hour incubation with the viruses, the medium was replaced with fresh complete medium. After 48 h, stably transduced cells were selected by adding puromycin to a final concentration of 5 µg/mL. The efficiency of gene knockdown or overexpression was subsequently validated by both RT-qPCR and Western blotting.
Cell proliferation and colony formation assays
The effect of
ZDHHC9
modulation on cell proliferation was evaluated using the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8; Dojindo Laboratories) assay. Briefly, stably transduced 143B, U2OS, and MG63 cells were seeded into 96-well plates at a density of 1 × 10^4 cells per well in seven replicates. At specified time points (24, 48, 72, and 96 h), CCK-8 solution was added to each well, and the plates were incubated for an additional hour. The absorbance at 450 nm was then measured using a microplate reader to determine cell viability.
The long-term proliferative capacity was assessed by a colony formation assay. Stably transduced cells were plated in six-well plates at a low density of 500 cells per well and maintained for two weeks, with the culture medium refreshed every three days. After the incubation period, the resulting colonies were washed with PBS, fixed for 15 min with 4% paraformaldehyde, and stained for 20 min with 1% crystal violet. Colonies containing more than 30 cells were then counted under an inverted microscope. All assays were performed in triplicate.
Wound healing assay
The migratory ability of osteosarcoma cells was assessed by an in vitro wound healing assay. For this, cells were seeded in 6-well plates and grown until they formed a nearly confluent (approximately 90%) monolayer. A sterile pipette tip was then used to create a linear scratch, or ‘wound’, across the center of the monolayer. After gently washing with PBS to remove any detached cells, the plates were replenished with serum-free medium to inhibit proliferation. Images of the wound area were acquired at 0, 12, and 24 h post-scratching using a microscope at 100× magnification. The extent of cell migration was determined by calculating the percentage of wound closure using the formula: [(Initial area – Final area) / Initial area] × 100%.
Transwell migration and invasion assays
The migratory and invasive capabilities of osteosarcoma cells were further evaluated using Transwell chambers (8 μm pore size; Corning). For both assays, 1 × 10
4
cells suspended in serum-free medium were seeded into the top chamber (the insert). The bottom chamber was filled with complete medium containing fetal bovine serum (FBS), which served as the chemoattractant; 10% FBS was used for migration assays and 20% FBS for invasion assays. For the invasion assay only, the inserts were first coated with a layer of diluted Matrigel (BD Biosciences) and incubated for at least 2 h at 37 °C to create an artificial basement membrane.
After a 48-hour incubation period, cells remaining on the upper surface of the membrane were carefully removed with a cotton swab. Cells that had migrated or invaded through the pores to the lower surface were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 10 min and subsequently stained with 0.1% crystal violet for 20 min. For quantification, the number of stained cells was counted in five random fields under a microscope. Each experiment was conducted in triplicate.
Cell cycle and apoptosis analysis
For cell cycle analysis, osteosarcoma cells were harvested and fixed overnight at 4 °C in ice-cold 75% ethanol. The fixed cells were then washed with PBS and treated with 1 mg/mL RNase A for 40 min at 37 °C. Subsequently, cells were stained with a propidium iodide (PI) solution (100 µg/mL; KeyGen Biotech) for 20 min in the dark. The distribution of cells in the G1, S, and G2/M phases was determined by flow cytometry (BD FACSCalibur), with data analysis performed using ModFit software.
Apoptosis was assessed using an Annexin V-FITC/PI Detection Kit (UElandy, Suzhou, China) following the manufacturer’s protocol. Briefly, approximately 5 × 10
5
cells were collected, washed twice with PBS, and resuspended in 1× binding buffer. The cells were then stained with 5 µL of Annexin V-FITC and 5 µL of PI, followed by a 15-minute incubation in the dark. The stained populations were promptly analyzed by flow cytometry (BD FACSCalibur), and the resulting data were processed with FlowJo software to quantify the percentages of early apoptotic, late apoptotic, and live cells.
Animal experiments and in vivo imaging
This study is reported in accordance with ARRIVE guidelines. All animal experiments were performed in accordance with the relevant guidelines and regulations and were approved by the Ethics Committee of the General Hospital of Ningxia Medical University.
Six-week-old male BALB/c nude mice, with an average body weight of 20 ± 2 g, were purchased from Wuhan Servicebio Technology Co., Ltd. (Wuhan, China). The mice were randomly assigned into three groups (n = 5 per group): a control group (LV-Control), a ZDHHC9 knockdown group (sh-
ZDHHC9
), and a rescue group (sh-
ZDHHC9
+ LV-
KRAS
). For tumor implantation, osteosarcoma cells (1 × 10⁷ cells/mL PBS) from the corresponding treatment groups were subcutaneously injected into the right flank of each mouse (0.1 mL). Tumor size was measured weekly, and tumor volume was calculated using the formula: V = (a × b²)/2, where ‘a’ is the largest diameter and ‘b’ is the smallest diameter.
For in vivo imaging procedures, mice were anesthetized using inhaled isoflurane. Twenty-four hours before the experiment, osteosarcoma cells transfected with a fluorescent label (1 × 10⁶ cells/100 µL PBS) were subcutaneously injected into the right dorsal flank of 6-week-old male BALB/c nude mice. In vivo imaging was performed every 3 days post-injection to monitor tumor growth and metastasis. Mice were intraperitoneally injected with 150 mg/kg D-Luciferin (Promega, USA) as a substrate and imaged 10 min later using the IVIS Spectrum CT system in fluorescence mode. Image data were analyzed and quantified using Living Image software (PerkinElmer, USA) to assess tumor growth dynamics.
At the experimental endpoint on day 31, all mice were euthanized. The procedure involved deep anesthetization with inhaled isoflurane, followed by CO₂ asphyxiation. Tumors were then collected, weighed, and fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde or stored in liquid nitrogen for further experiments.
Statistical analysis
All experiments were independently repeated three times. Data were analyzed using GraphPad Prism 10 software. Continuous variables following a normal distribution are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD). Comparisons between two groups were performed using an unpaired two-tailed Student’s
t
-test. Comparisons among multiple groups were performed using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s multiple comparisons test. Non-normally distributed data were analyzed using the Mann-Whitney U test. Categorical variables are expressed as counts (n) and percentages (%). Comparisons of proportions between groups were performed using the chi-square (χ
2
test or Fisher’s exact test. Normality was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test or the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. A
P
-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Introduction
Osteosarcoma (OS) is a primary malignant bone tumor that predominantly affects children and adolescents. The global incidence of osteosarcoma is approximately 3.9 cases per million individuals annually, resulting in an estimated 21,000 deaths worldwide
1
–
3
. The current standard of care for osteosarcoma encompasses neoadjuvant chemotherapy, surgical resection, and adjuvant chemotherapy. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy, administered prior to surgical resection, aims to reduce tumor volume and enhance surgical success rates
4
–
6
. Surgical resection remains the cornerstone of treatment, with the objective of achieving complete tumor removal
7
. Adjuvant chemotherapy, administered post-operatively, serves to eradicate residual tumor cells and mitigate the risk of recurrence
8
. Despite this multimodal treatment approach, the five-year survival rate for patients with metastatic osteosarcoma remains below 30%
5
,
9
,
10
. This unfavorable prognosis is primarily attributed to tumor cell resistance to conventional chemotherapeutic agents
11
and the lack of effective molecular biomarkers to guide personalized treatment strategies
12
. Therefore, a deeper understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying osteosarcoma initiation, progression, and metastasis, coupled with the identification of novel therapeutic targets and prognostic biomarkers, is crucial for improving patient outcomes.
The zinc finger DHHC-type protein (ZDHHC) family comprises a group of protein palmitoyltransferases characterized by an Asp-His-His-Cys (DHHC) domain. These enzymes catalyze protein palmitoylation, a post-translational modification that regulates the membrane localization, protein-protein interactions, and signal transduction of target proteins
13
,
14
. ZDHHC9, a prominent member of the ZDHHC family, has been implicated in the pathogenesis of various cancers
15
For instance, ZDHHC9 promotes tumor immune evasion in breast cancer by stabilizing PD-L1
16
, enhances the Warburg effect in glioblastoma by activating GLUT1
17
, and maintains KRAS activity in leukemia by promoting its membrane localization
18
. Furthermore, aberrant ZDHHC9 expression has been reported in several other cancers, including lung cancer
19
colorectal cancer
20
and bladder cancer
21
where it contributes to tumorigenesis and progression. These studies highlight the complex and diverse regulatory functions of ZDHHC9 in different tumor types, potentially influencing tumor cell metabolism, signal transduction, and immune evasion
22
. However, the role of ZDHHC9 in osteosarcoma and its underlying molecular mechanisms remain unexplored. Given the established role of ZDHHC9 in promoting tumorigenesis and immune evasion in multiple cancer types, investigating its function in osteosarcoma is of significant importance for identifying novel therapeutic targets and prognostic biomarkers.

Standard IHC procedures were followed to detect ZDHHC9 expression. Briefly, sections were deparaffinized in xylene, rehydrated through a graded ethanol series, and subjected to antigen retrieval in pH 6.0 citrate buffer at 95 °C for 15 min. Endogenous peroxidase activity was blocked with 3% hydrogen peroxide for 10 min at room temperature. After blocking with 5% bovine serum albumin (BSA), sections were incubated with primary antibody (1:100, Cat NO: 24046-1-AP-50, Proteintech, Wuhan, China) overnight at 4 °C. After washing with PBS, sections were incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibody (1:200, Cat NO: GB23303, Servicebio, Wuhan, China) for 1 h at room temperature. DAB was used as the chromogen, and nuclei were counterstained with hematoxylin. Stained sections were observed and imaged using a Motic microscope (Beijing, China), and staining indices were measured and calculated using Image-Pro Plus 6 software. Negative controls were performed using phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) instead of the primary antibody. ZDHHC9 staining intensity was graded as 0 (negative), 1 (weak), 2 (moderate), or 3 (strong). The percentage of positively stained cells was scored as 0 (≤ 5%), 1 (6–25%), 2 (26–50%), 3 (51–75%), and 4 (> 75%). The final staining score (0–12) was calculated by multiplying the staining intensity and percentage scores. The scores were categorized as follows: –, 0 points; +, 1–4 points; ++, 5–8 points; +++, 9–12 points.
Western blot analysis
For immunoblotting, protein lysates were prepared from tissues and cells using RIPA lysis buffer supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors. The total protein concentration of each lysate was determined via a BCA Protein Assay Kit. An equal amount of protein (30 µg) from each sample was resolved on 10% or 12% SDS-PAGE gels and subsequently transferred onto polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membranes. Following the transfer, membranes were blocked for 1 h at room temperature in 5% non-fat milk dissolved in TBST. The membranes were then probed overnight at 4 °C with specific primary antibodies. After washing three times with TBST, membranes were incubated with the corresponding secondary antibodies, and immunoreactive bands were visualized using an enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL) kit. Densitometric analysis of the bands was performed using ImageJ software. To ensure equal loading, protein levels were normalized to GAPDH. All immunoblotting experiments were conducted in triplicate, and representative blots are presented in the figures.Antibodies against ZDHHC9 (1:3000, 82739-1-RR), KRAS (1:1000, 12063-1-AP), ERK1/2 (1:2500, 83533-1-RR), and p-ERK1/2 (1:500, 80031-1-RR) were purchased from Proteintech (Wuhan, China). GAPDH (1:5000, GB15004-100) antibody was purchased from Servicebio, Wuhan, China. Antibodies against CDK4 (1:1000, DF6102), CDK6 (1:1000, DF6448), p27 (1:1000, DF6090), P21 (1:1000, DF6423), P53 (1:1000, AF0879), Snail (1:500, AF6032), Twist1 (1:500, AF4009), Cleaved-Caspase 3 (1:500, AF7022), and Cleaved-Caspase 9 (1:500, AF5240) were purchased from Affinity Biosciences (USA). Antibodies against PCNA (1:1000, A12427) and Ki-67 (1:500, A11390) were purchased from ABclonal (China). Antibody against Slug (1:500, BS79813) was purchased from Nanjing Baiaolaibo Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (China).
Real-time quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR)
The mRNA expression levels of target genes were measured by real-time quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR). Following the manufacturer’s protocol, total RNA was first isolated from cells using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen). Subsequently, cDNA was synthesized from 1 µg of total RNA with the PrimeScript
®
RT Reagent Kit (Takara Biotech). The qPCR reactions were then performed using a SYBR Green master mix (Vazyme) on a real-time PCR system. Relative gene expression was calculated using the 2
−ΔΔCt
method, with
GAPDH
serving as the endogenous control for normalization. The primer sequences used for amplification were as follows:
ZDHHC9
forward 5′-ATGGCTACACTGTTGAGGAC-3′, reverse 5′-ATTCTTGATACGAGGCGGTG-3′;
GAPDH
forward 5′-ACATCGCTCAGACACCATG-3′, reverse 5′-TGTAGTTGAGGTCAATGAAGGG-3′.
Cell culture
The human osteosarcoma cell lines 143B, U2OS, Saos-2, and MG63, the human fetal osteoblast cell line hFOB 1.19, and human spinal mesenchymal stem cells (hMSC) were all purchased from the Cell Bank of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. The osteosarcoma lines 143B, U2OS, and MG63 were maintained in high-glucose DMEM (Gibco, USA), while Saos-2 cells were grown in RPMI 1640 medium (Gibco). The hFOB 1.19 cell line was cultured in DMEM/F12 medium (Gibco) containing 2.5 mM L-glutamine and 0.3 mg/mL G418 (Sigma-Aldrich). hMSCs were cultured using a specialized hMSC Serum-Free Medium Kit. With the exception of the hMSC medium, all other culture media were supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS, Biowest), 100 U/mL penicillin, and 0.1 mg/mL streptomycin (Leagene Biotechnology). All cell lines were maintained at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO₂.
Transfection
Lentiviral vectors for knockdown and overexpression were obtained from Qingke Biotechnology Co., Ltd. These included a short hairpin RNA targeting
ZDHHC9
(sh-
ZDHHC9
), a non-targeting negative control (sh-NC), an overexpression plasmid for
ZDHHC9
(LV-
ZDHHC9
), an overexpression plasmid for
KRAS
(LV-
KRAS
), and a corresponding empty vector (LV-Control). For lentiviral transduction, osteosarcoma cells were plated in six-well plates at a density of 1 × 10^5 cells/well 24 h prior to infection. Cells were then transduced with the respective lentiviruses at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) determined by the supplier’s instructions. A rescue group was established by co-infecting cells with sh-
ZDHHC9
and LV-
KRAS
lentiviruses. Following a 12-hour incubation with the viruses, the medium was replaced with fresh complete medium. After 48 h, stably transduced cells were selected by adding puromycin to a final concentration of 5 µg/mL. The efficiency of gene knockdown or overexpression was subsequently validated by both RT-qPCR and Western blotting.
Cell proliferation and colony formation assays
The effect of
ZDHHC9
modulation on cell proliferation was evaluated using the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8; Dojindo Laboratories) assay. Briefly, stably transduced 143B, U2OS, and MG63 cells were seeded into 96-well plates at a density of 1 × 10^4 cells per well in seven replicates. At specified time points (24, 48, 72, and 96 h), CCK-8 solution was added to each well, and the plates were incubated for an additional hour. The absorbance at 450 nm was then measured using a microplate reader to determine cell viability.
The long-term proliferative capacity was assessed by a colony formation assay. Stably transduced cells were plated in six-well plates at a low density of 500 cells per well and maintained for two weeks, with the culture medium refreshed every three days. After the incubation period, the resulting colonies were washed with PBS, fixed for 15 min with 4% paraformaldehyde, and stained for 20 min with 1% crystal violet. Colonies containing more than 30 cells were then counted under an inverted microscope. All assays were performed in triplicate.
Wound healing assay
The migratory ability of osteosarcoma cells was assessed by an in vitro wound healing assay. For this, cells were seeded in 6-well plates and grown until they formed a nearly confluent (approximately 90%) monolayer. A sterile pipette tip was then used to create a linear scratch, or ‘wound’, across the center of the monolayer. After gently washing with PBS to remove any detached cells, the plates were replenished with serum-free medium to inhibit proliferation. Images of the wound area were acquired at 0, 12, and 24 h post-scratching using a microscope at 100× magnification. The extent of cell migration was determined by calculating the percentage of wound closure using the formula: [(Initial area – Final area) / Initial area] × 100%.
Transwell migration and invasion assays
The migratory and invasive capabilities of osteosarcoma cells were further evaluated using Transwell chambers (8 μm pore size; Corning). For both assays, 1 × 10
4
cells suspended in serum-free medium were seeded into the top chamber (the insert). The bottom chamber was filled with complete medium containing fetal bovine serum (FBS), which served as the chemoattractant; 10% FBS was used for migration assays and 20% FBS for invasion assays. For the invasion assay only, the inserts were first coated with a layer of diluted Matrigel (BD Biosciences) and incubated for at least 2 h at 37 °C to create an artificial basement membrane.
After a 48-hour incubation period, cells remaining on the upper surface of the membrane were carefully removed with a cotton swab. Cells that had migrated or invaded through the pores to the lower surface were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 10 min and subsequently stained with 0.1% crystal violet for 20 min. For quantification, the number of stained cells was counted in five random fields under a microscope. Each experiment was conducted in triplicate.
Cell cycle and apoptosis analysis
For cell cycle analysis, osteosarcoma cells were harvested and fixed overnight at 4 °C in ice-cold 75% ethanol. The fixed cells were then washed with PBS and treated with 1 mg/mL RNase A for 40 min at 37 °C. Subsequently, cells were stained with a propidium iodide (PI) solution (100 µg/mL; KeyGen Biotech) for 20 min in the dark. The distribution of cells in the G1, S, and G2/M phases was determined by flow cytometry (BD FACSCalibur), with data analysis performed using ModFit software.
Apoptosis was assessed using an Annexin V-FITC/PI Detection Kit (UElandy, Suzhou, China) following the manufacturer’s protocol. Briefly, approximately 5 × 10
5
cells were collected, washed twice with PBS, and resuspended in 1× binding buffer. The cells were then stained with 5 µL of Annexin V-FITC and 5 µL of PI, followed by a 15-minute incubation in the dark. The stained populations were promptly analyzed by flow cytometry (BD FACSCalibur), and the resulting data were processed with FlowJo software to quantify the percentages of early apoptotic, late apoptotic, and live cells.
Animal experiments and in vivo imaging
This study is reported in accordance with ARRIVE guidelines. All animal experiments were performed in accordance with the relevant guidelines and regulations and were approved by the Ethics Committee of the General Hospital of Ningxia Medical University.
Six-week-old male BALB/c nude mice, with an average body weight of 20 ± 2 g, were purchased from Wuhan Servicebio Technology Co., Ltd. (Wuhan, China). The mice were randomly assigned into three groups (n = 5 per group): a control group (LV-Control), a ZDHHC9 knockdown group (sh-
ZDHHC9
), and a rescue group (sh-
ZDHHC9
+ LV-
KRAS
). For tumor implantation, osteosarcoma cells (1 × 10⁷ cells/mL PBS) from the corresponding treatment groups were subcutaneously injected into the right flank of each mouse (0.1 mL). Tumor size was measured weekly, and tumor volume was calculated using the formula: V = (a × b²)/2, where ‘a’ is the largest diameter and ‘b’ is the smallest diameter.
For in vivo imaging procedures, mice were anesthetized using inhaled isoflurane. Twenty-four hours before the experiment, osteosarcoma cells transfected with a fluorescent label (1 × 10⁶ cells/100 µL PBS) were subcutaneously injected into the right dorsal flank of 6-week-old male BALB/c nude mice. In vivo imaging was performed every 3 days post-injection to monitor tumor growth and metastasis. Mice were intraperitoneally injected with 150 mg/kg D-Luciferin (Promega, USA) as a substrate and imaged 10 min later using the IVIS Spectrum CT system in fluorescence mode. Image data were analyzed and quantified using Living Image software (PerkinElmer, USA) to assess tumor growth dynamics.
At the experimental endpoint on day 31, all mice were euthanized. The procedure involved deep anesthetization with inhaled isoflurane, followed by CO₂ asphyxiation. Tumors were then collected, weighed, and fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde or stored in liquid nitrogen for further experiments.
Statistical analysis
All experiments were independently repeated three times. Data were analyzed using GraphPad Prism 10 software. Continuous variables following a normal distribution are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD). Comparisons between two groups were performed using an unpaired two-tailed Student’s
t
-test. Comparisons among multiple groups were performed using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s multiple comparisons test. Non-normally distributed data were analyzed using the Mann-Whitney U test. Categorical variables are expressed as counts (n) and percentages (%). Comparisons of proportions between groups were performed using the chi-square (χ
2
test or Fisher’s exact test. Normality was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test or the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. A
P
-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Discussion
ZDHHC (Zinc finger DHHC-type containing) proteins are ubiquitously expressed in eukaryotes and are responsible for catalyzing the post-translational modification of proteins, thereby influencing their function and localization
23
. Their crucial roles in physiological processes, including cell proliferation, differentiation, development, and cell death, have garnered extensive research interest
24
. Twenty-three human ZDHHC proteins (ZDHHC1-24) have been identified, all of which contain a conserved DHHC cysteine-rich domain (DHHC-CRD)
25
,
26
. Recent studies have increasingly focused on the roles of ZDHHC family proteins in the initiation and progression of tumors
27
.
ZDHHC9, a member of the ZDHHC family, is also known as CXorf11 and ZNF379. The gene is located within an open reading frame on chromosome Xq26.1. Its catalytic domain contains the conserved DHHC sequence, enabling it to regulate the function of various proteins, including their localization, stability, and signal transduction capabilities
28
. Although studies have indicated that ZDHHC9 exhibits pro-oncogenic activity in various malignancies, including breast cancer, lung cancer, and glioblastoma, and is associated with patient clinical outcomes and aggressive characteristics of cancer cells
29
its significance and precise mechanisms in osteosarcoma have remained undefined. Consistent with the aforementioned studies, our research revealed increased expression of ZDHHC9 in osteosarcoma tissues and cell lines, and a strong correlation was observed between elevated
ZDHHC9
levels and worsened prognosis in patients diagnosed with osteosarcoma. Therefore,
ZDHHC9
may represent a risk factor and an independent prognostic biomarker for osteosarcoma. Furthermore, the depletion of
ZDHHC9
led to diminished proliferation, migration, and invasion of osteosarcoma cells, and hindered tumor growth in vivo. Conversely,
ZDHHC9
overexpression stimulated cell proliferation, migration, and invasion, providing further evidence for its role in tumorigenesis. Thus, our study unveils
ZDHHC9
as a potential biomarker and oncogene in osteosarcoma.
To gain deeper insights into how
ZDHHC9
promotes cell proliferation, migration, and invasion, and considering the possibility that ZDHHC9, as a protein post-translational modification factor, controls these processes, we initially analyzed genes significantly associated with
ZDHHC9
expression through proteomic sequencing. Subsequently, GO and KEGG enrichment analyses indicated a high degree of enrichment in the Ras/MAPK signaling pathway. This finding suggests that
ZDHHC9
may play a pivotal role in this signaling cascade. Further PPI protein interaction analysis using the STRING database (
www.string-db.org
) revealed that
ZDHHC9
may regulate the RAS/MAPK signaling pathway through
KRAS
, providing further support for
ZDHHC9’
s regulatory function in this pathway.
The Ras/MAPK signaling pathway is a critical intracellular signal transduction pathway involved in regulating various fundamental cellular processes, including cell growth, differentiation, survival, and apoptosis
30
. The core components of this pathway include Ras proteins (
KRAS
,
NRAS
, and
HRAS
), Raf kinases (ARaf, BRaf, and CRaf), MEK1/2 kinases, and ERK1/2 kinases
31
.
KRAS
, acting as a molecular switch, cycles between an inactive GDP-bound state and an active GTP-bound state. Activation of growth factor receptors (such as EGFR) can recruit guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs, such as SOS), promoting the conversion of Ras-GDP to Ras-GTP. Activated Ras-GTP then binds to and activates Raf kinases, which phosphorylate and activate MEK1/2. MEK1/2, in turn, phosphorylates and activates ERK1/2. Activated ERK1/2 translocates to the nucleus, phosphorylating various transcription factors and regulating gene expression
32
,
33
. The role of the Ras/MAPK pathway in cancer is multifaceted. On one hand, this pathway can act as a tumor suppressor; for example, sustained ERK activation can induce cellular senescence or apoptosis in certain contexts
34
. On the other hand, the Ras/MAPK pathway more frequently functions as a pro-oncogenic pathway, with mutations or hyperactivation of its components commonly observed in various human cancers
35
,
36
. For instance, mutations in
KRAS
,
NRAS
, and
BRaf
are highly prevalent in pancreatic cancer, colorectal cancer, and melanoma
37
. Consequently, the Ras/MAPK pathway has become a significant target for cancer therapy, and inhibitors targeting different nodes of this pathway have entered clinical trials or have been approved for clinical use
38
,
39
.
To elucidate the function of ZDHHC9 in the Ras/MAPK signaling pathway, we examined the expression levels of
KRAS
,
Raf1
,
ERK1/2
, and
p-ERK1/2
. Our results demonstrate that
ZDHHC9
overexpression enhances the expression of KRAS, Raf1, ERK1/2, and p-ERK1/2 in osteosarcoma cells, which is associated with increased expression of Ki67, PCNA, Cyclin D1, and CDK4, key factors in tumor proliferation and migration
29
. Conversely,
ZDHHC9
knockdown reduces the expression of
KRAS
,
Raf1
,
ERK1/2
, and
p-ERK1/2
in osteosarcoma cells, thereby decreasing the expression of Ki67, PCNA, Cyclin D1, and CDK4. More importantly, we found that simultaneous knockdown of
ZDHHC9
and overexpression of
KRAS
in 143B and U2OS cells partially abrogated the effects of
ZDHHC9
knockdown on osteosarcoma cell proliferation, migration, and invasion. This was further corroborated by animal experiments. These results indicate that upregulated
ZDHHC9
in osteosarcoma promotes tumor proliferation and migration by enhancing the activity of the Ras/MAPK pathway, leading to increased expression of Ki67, PCNA, Cyclin D1, and CDK4.
In summary, our study provides the first evidence of
ZDHHC9
upregulation in osteosarcoma, and this upregulation is associated with poor prognosis in osteosarcoma patients.
ZDHHC9
enhances osteosarcoma cell proliferation, migration, and invasion by enhancing the Ras/MAPK signaling pathway. This suggests that
ZDHHC9
may represent a novel therapeutic target for the treatment of osteosarcoma.
It is also important to position our findings within the broader context of osteosarcoma’s complex regulatory landscape. In addition to the post-translational modifications we investigated, other regulatory networks, such as those involving non-coding RNAs, are known to play crucial roles in osteosarcoma pathogenesis. For instance, studies have shown that long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) can function as competing endogenous RNAs (ceRNAs) to ‘sponge’ microRNAs (miRNAs), thereby modulating target gene expression and driving disease progression
40
. The potential interplay between the ZDHHC9-KRAS protein axis and these non-coding RNA regulatory networks presents an interesting avenue for future research, which could unveil a more comprehensive map of the molecular drivers in this disease.
Our study has several limitations that warrant consideration. A key limitation is the lack of direct evidence for KRAS palmitoylation by ZDHHC9 in osteosarcoma cells. While our co-immunoprecipitation results confirm an interaction and our functional assays show a strong association between ZDHHC9 and enhanced RAS/MAPK pathway activity, the precise mechanism remains to be fully elucidated. Future studies, such as palmitoylation assays and the analysis of KRAS membrane localization following
ZDHHC9
modulation, are necessary to confirm that this regulation occurs via direct post-translational modification. Additionally, whether ZDHHC9 participates in other oncogenic processes in osteosarcoma requires further investigation.
